lead: A V-belt sits in a grooved pulley and wedges into it. The wedge raises the effective friction from μ to about μ / sin β, roughly three times, so the drive grips with a short centre distance and small pulleys. The price is that one belt carries only a few kilowatts; the drive is rated as a number of standard belts. V-belts run pumps, compressors, fans and machine tools, including many Indian workshop drives.
prereq: You need: the tension ratio and power relation from design of flat belt drives, and belt construction from flexible drives and belt materials.

blocks.text: A flat belt grips only on the pulley rim. A V-belt grips on its two side faces, which press against the sides of a groove. If the belt is pushed into the groove with a radial force R, each side face pushes back with a normal force R<sub>n</sub>, and only the radial parts of those two forces balance R: 2R<sub>n</sub> sin β = R. The friction available is 2μR<sub>n</sub> = μR/sin β, larger than the μR a flat rim would give. So the flat-belt tension ratio applies with μ replaced by the effective friction μ′.

blocks.where: β is the half groove angle; μ is the real coefficient of friction between belt and pulley; μ′ is the effective friction.

T₁ and T₂ are the tight-side and slack-side tensions that produce friction, in N, as for flat belts; the total pull in the tight side is T₁ + T<sub>c</sub>. θ is the arc of contact on the small pulley in radians and β is the half groove angle.

blocks.text: For 2β = 38°, β = 19° and sin 19° = 0.326, so μ′ ≈ 3.07μ. This is why a V-drive works on short centres and small pulleys. The belt’s own angle is 40°; the groove is cut at 34° to 38°, narrowest on small pulleys, so the bent belt still bears on both sides. A V-flat drive runs V-belts in a grooved small pulley and on a plain large one, often a flywheel, for large ratios on short centres.

V-belts come in standard sections. The letter gives the cross-section and the number gives the belt length in millimetres, usually the pitch length. Thus B 1000 is a B-section belt 1000 mm long. Pitch length is measured on the pitch line, the line inside the belt that does not change length when the belt bends.

Larger sections carry more power but need larger pulleys. For a first choice, use a selection chart that plots design power against small-pulley speed for each section. The belt speed is v = πdN/60, where d is the small-pulley pitch diameter in metres, N its speed in rev/min and v is in m/s. Classical V-belts are kept below about 25 to 30 m/s: above that, the centrifugal tension T<sub>c</sub> = m v² (m is belt mass per metre) eats the grip and the belt flexes too often.

A smaller section can run on a smaller pulley and at higher speed, but needs more belts. Do not mix sections on one pulley set. Tensioning is by sliding the motor on rails or by an idler; check deflection at mid-span.

Design starts with the duty. The service factor F<sub>a</sub> accounts for shock and running hours. Design power P<sub>d</sub> = F<sub>a</sub> P, where P is the motor power in kW and P<sub>d</sub> is the power the belts must be rated for. A smooth electric motor driving a compressor for two shifts may need F<sub>a</sub> = 1.2; a crusher may need 1.5 or more.

items: Choose the section from P<sub>d</sub> and the small-pulley speed.
Choose a small pulley above the minimum for the section; find the large pulley from the speed ratio.
Find the arc of contact and the pitch length; take the nearest standard length.
Read the rated power P<sub>r</sub> per belt at the small-pulley speed and diameter.
Find the arc factor K<sub>θ</sub> and the length factor K<sub>L</sub>.
z = P<sub>d</sub> / (P<sub>r</sub> K<sub>θ</sub> K<sub>L</sub>); round up.

blocks.text: z = Pd / (Pr Kθ KL), where z is the number of belts, Pd the design power in kW, Pr the rated power per belt in kW, Kθ the arc-of-contact factor and KL the belt-length factor.

P<sub>r</sub> is read for a 180° arc and a standard length. K<sub>θ</sub> is below 1 when θ is under 180°. K<sub>L</sub> is below 1 for a shorter belt, which passes round the pulleys more often each second and fatigues sooner, and above 1 for a longer one. Keep z at about 8 or fewer, or move to a bigger section or larger pulleys. Several belts share the load evenly only as a matched set, tensioned together.

figure.caption: The groove multiplies friction, and the worked example rounds the belt count up. Each side pushes back with a reaction that leans at β, so the friction is μR/sin β; four belts give 8.60 kW, short of 9.0 kW, so five are used.

spec.aria: V-belt in a 38 degree groove with the radial push R and two side reactions; beside it, bars of 4 and 5 belts at 2.149 kilowatts each against a 9.0 kilowatt design power line.

examples.question: A 7.5 kW, 1440 rpm motor drives a reciprocating compressor at 480 rpm for two shifts of 8 h a day. Select a B-section V-belt drive with pitch diameters 140 mm and 420 mm and a centre distance of 420 mm. The rating chart gives 2.6 kW per belt; the arc factor is 0.87 and the length factor 0.95. Take a service factor of 1.2. Find the pitch length and the number of belts.
steps: Belt speed v = πdN₁/60 = π × 0.140 × 1440/60 = 10.56 m/s, below 25 m/s.

Pitch length: L = 2C + π(D + d)/2 + (D − d)²/(4C) = 840 + π × 560/2 + 280²/1680 = 840 + 879.6 + 46.7 = 1766.3 mm. Order the nearest standard pitch length from the maker’s list and reset the centre distance to suit; the length factor 0.95 applies to that belt.
Corrected rating per belt = P<sub>r</sub>K<sub>θ</sub>K<sub>L</sub> = 2.6 × 0.87 × 0.95 = 2.149 kW.
Number of belts z = 9.0/2.149 = 4.19. Four belts give only 4 × 2.149 = 8.60 kW, short of 9.0 kW, so use 5 belts (10.74 kW).
examples.answer: Pitch length about 1766 mm (nearest standard length); use 5 B-section belts.
examples.check:
import math
Pd = 1.2*7.5; d, D, C, N1 = 140.0, 420.0, 420.0, 1440.0
v = math.pi*d/1000*N1/60
al = math.degrees(math.asin((D - d)/(2*C))); th = 180 - 2*al
L = 2*C + math.pi*(D + d)/2 + (D - d)**2/(4*C)
pr = 2.6*0.87*0.95; z = Pd/pr
print(Pd, round(v, 2), round(al, 2), round(th, 2), round(L, 1), round(pr, 3), round(z, 2), math.ceil(z))

examples.question: For the same drive, check the belts by tension instead of by chart. Each B-section belt has a mass of 0.19 kg/m and a safe working tension of 300 N; μ = 0.2 between belt and pulley and the groove angle is 38°. Find the power one belt can carry and the number of belts for 9.0 kW.
steps: Half groove angle β = 19°, sin β = 0.3256. Effective friction μ′ = 0.2/0.3256 = 0.614.
Arc on the small pulley from worked example 1: θ = 2.462 rad. So μ′θ = 0.614 × 2.462 = 1.512 and e<sup>1.512</sup> = 4.54. (A flat belt with μ = 0.2 would have only e<sup>0.492</sup> = 1.64.)
Centrifugal tension: T<sub>c</sub> = m v² = 0.19 × 10.56² = 21.2 N.
Friction tension on the tight side: T₁ = 300 − 21.2 = 278.8 N. Slack side: T₂ = 278.8/4.54 = 61.4 N.
examples.answer: One belt carries 2.29 kW, so the tension check asks for 4 belts. The chart method asked for 5 because its rating also allows for fatigue life; when both are worked, the design takes the larger count, 5 belts.
examples.check:
import math
v = math.pi*0.14*1440/60
th = math.radians(180 - 2*math.degrees(math.asin(280/840)))
k = math.exp(0.2/math.sin(math.radians(19))*th)
Tc = 0.19*v**2; T1 = 300 - Tc; T2 = T1/k
P = (T1 - T2)*v
print(round(k, 2), round(Tc, 1), round(T1, 1), round(T2, 1), round(P), round(9000/P, 2))

traps: Using the full groove angle in sin β. For 2β = 38°, sin 19° = 0.326, not sin 38° = 0.616; the wrong value roughly halves μ′.
Forgetting the service factor. The belts must carry P<sub>d</sub> = F<sub>a</sub>P, not the motor power P.
Using millimetres in v = πdN/60. Put d in metres, or the speed comes out 1000 times too large.
Rounding the number of belts down. 4.19 means 5 belts; 4 belts carry only 8.60 kW against 9.0 kW.
Using the flat-belt ratio e<sup>μθ</sup> for a V-belt. The V-belt exponent is μθ/sin β: 4.54 instead of 1.64 in worked example 2.

quiz.q: What does the designation B 1000 mean?
Why does a V-belt carry more power than a flat belt of the same width?
quiz.a: The V-belt wedges into the groove, so the normal force on its two side faces is larger than the radial push. The effective friction is μ/sin β, about three times μ for β = 19°.

quiz.q: A V-belt has μ = 0.3 and half groove angle β = 19°. Find μ′.
Why does the groove angle narrow on small pulleys?
quiz.a: When the belt bends round a small pulley, its stretched top narrows and its squeezed bottom widens, so the angle between its sides becomes smaller than 40°. A narrower groove keeps both side faces in contact, so the wedge and the friction are kept.

quiz.q: Find belt speed for d = 100 mm and N = 1500 rpm.
The calculated number of belts is 7.6. What do you do?
quiz.a: Round up to 8 belts. Eight is at the usual limit; if the count were above 8, use a larger section, larger pulleys or two drives.

quiz.q: Why is the length factor below 1 for a short belt?
quiz.a: A short belt bends more times per second for the same speed, so it fatigues faster and its rated power is reduced.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry uses standard selection charts, raw-edge cogged belts and variable-speed V-belt drives; tension gauges and vibration checks set the take-up. V-flat and multi-groove drives are common on fans and pumps. Search 'V-belt drive selection ISO 4184', 'V-flat drive' and 'belt tension gauge'.
